explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. God says, "Son of man, set your face against the mountains of Israel and prophesy against them." (Ezekiel 6:2) Son of man is what God calls Ezekiel throughout this passage. So Ezekiel gets his orders: turn and face the mountains, and speak. Not the easiest audience to preach to, but a prophet goes where he's sent.

Nineveh was a big city, but it isn't in this message. God tells Ezekiel, a priest living among the exiles, to set his face against "the mountains of Israel" (Ezekiel 6:2). Ezekiel isn't pointed at walls at all, but at mountains, which is odd enough that it sticks with you. Nice guess on the walls, though. I once guessed a recipe by smell and ended up with a very confident mistake.

Babylon is where Ezekiel's neighbors are living as exiles, so I see why it came to mind. But God doesn't point him at any gates. He says, "Son of man, set your face against the mountains of Israel and prophesy against them." (Ezekiel 6:2) The message is for the mountains back home, and Ezekiel delivers it from far away.

Yes, friend! God says, "I am about to bring a sword against you, and I will destroy your high places." (Ezekiel 6:3) The high places were spots up on the hills where the people worshiped idols, and verse 13 mentions the high hills as places where they offered incense to those idols. So the sword is headed straight for those hilltop spots.

Palaces make sense if you're picturing a sword aimed at kings, but that's not what God says here. He says, "I am about to bring a sword against you, and I will destroy your high places." (Ezekiel 6:3) The high places were hilltop spots, and verse 13 ties the high hills to incense offered to idols. No palaces in this verse at all.

Watchtowers sound like a solid guess when a sword is coming. But the verse never mentions them. God says, "I am about to bring a sword against you, and I will destroy your high places." (Ezekiel 6:3) Those high places are where idols got worshiped, so that's what's on the list.

That's it. God says, "I will cast down your slain before your idols." (Ezekiel 6:4) Verse 5 says it again: He will lay the corpses of the Israelites before their idols. The very things they trusted are right there to watch it happen. It's a heavy part, so I'll just say it plainly: this one hurts.

Kings are a fair guess, since a lot of Bible stories have kings in the middle. But this verse says, "I will cast down your slain before your idols." (Ezekiel 6:4) No king is mentioned. It's heavy stuff, so I'll just say plainly that I think this one hurts, and the idols are the center of it.

I get why enemies came to mind with a sword in the picture. But the verse puts the focus somewhere else. God says, "I will cast down your slain before your idols." (Ezekiel 6:4) Verse 5 repeats it with the corpses laid before their idols. This is a heavy part of the message, and I think it's meant to hit hard.

Not quite, friend. God says the opposite: "Wherever you live, the cities will be laid waste…" (Ezekiel 6:6) Laid waste means they won't be left standing. The same verse says the high places will be demolished and the altars laid waste and desecrated. Nothing in this stretch leaves the cities standing.

Right, baker. The statement is false because God says, "Wherever you live, the cities will be laid waste…" (Ezekiel 6:6) So the cities don't stay standing. The high places, altars, idols and incense altars all go down in that same verse. It's a long list, and the cities are on it.

You got it, baker. God says, "The slain will fall among you, and you will know that I am the LORD." (Ezekiel 6:7) That line comes back again and again in this passage, in verses 10, 13 and 14. God keeps saying it, so it clearly matters. It's the point He keeps coming back to.

explanations.answer: That their army is too small
explanations.explanation: That's a reasonable thing to think when people are falling. But God doesn't say a word about an army here. He says, "The slain will fall among you, and you will know that I am the LORD." (Ezekiel 6:7) What they come to know is who God is. It's the line He repeats through the whole passage.

Kings aren't mentioned in this verse. God says, "The slain will fall among you, and you will know that I am the LORD." (Ezekiel 6:7) What they come to know is about God, not about their leaders. And He says it again in verses 10, 13 and 14, so it's easy to remember.

Yes, baker. God says, "Yet I will leave a remnant, for some of you will escape the sword when you are scattered among the nations and throughout the lands." (Ezekiel 6:8) A remnant is the part that's left. After all that smashing, that one little word opens a door.

Good news, friend, it's true. After all the hard words, God says, "Yet I will leave a remnant, for some of you will escape the sword when you are scattered among the nations and throughout the lands." (Ezekiel 6:8) A remnant is the part that's left over. So some do get away from the sword.

That's right. God says, "Then in the nations to which they have been carried captive, your survivors will remember Me…" (Ezekiel 6:9) Far from home, they turn their thoughts back to Him. Remembering is where it starts.

Kings are a natural guess, but the verse doesn't say that. God says, "Then in the nations to which they have been carried captive, your survivors will remember Me…" (Ezekiel 6:9) The "Me" is the LORD Himself. The survivors are far from home, and He's who they remember.

Not the prophets, friend. God says, "Then in the nations to which they have been carried captive, your survivors will remember Me…" (Ezekiel 6:9) He's talking about Himself. Even in captivity, the survivors think of the LORD.

That's the word. The verse says, "So they will loathe themselves for the evil they have done and for all their abominations." (Ezekiel 6:9) It comes right after they remember how He was grieved by their hearts that turned away. It's a heavy moment, and I think it's a sorrowful one.

Forgiving themselves would be easier, wouldn't it? But the verse goes a different way: "So they will loathe themselves for the evil they have done and for all their abominations." (Ezekiel 6:9) That comes after they remember how He was grieved by their adulterous hearts. It's a heavy line, and I think it's meant to be.

Making excuses is a very human move, I've done it with burnt batches. But that's not what happens here. The verse says, "So they will loathe themselves for the evil they have done and for all their abominations." (Ezekiel 6:9) No excuses, just honest sorrow over what they did.

Not so, friend. God says, "And they will know that I am the LORD; I did not declare in vain that I would bring this calamity upon them." (Ezekiel 6:10) In vain means for nothing. So what He said would happen was no empty threat, and they will know it.

That's right, baker. God says, "And they will know that I am the LORD; I did not declare in vain that I would bring this calamity upon them." (Ezekiel 6:10) He didn't say it for nothing. His word was real, and they will come to know it.

explanations.answer: Clap his hands and stomp his feet
explanations.explanation: That's the one. God says, "Clap your hands, stomp your feet, and cry out ‘Alas!’ because of all the wicked abominations of the house of Israel…" (Ezekiel 6:11) So Ezekiel gets a whole-body assignment. No sitting still for this prophet.

explanations.answer: Tear his robe and sit in ashes
explanations.explanation: Robe tearing and ashes are a real way people showed sorrow in the Bible, but that's not what God asks of Ezekiel here. He says, "Clap your hands, stomp your feet, and cry out ‘Alas!’…" (Ezekiel 6:11) So it's clapping and stomping, not ashes. I'd say that's a pretty loud assignment.

explanations.answer: Lie on his side for many days
explanations.explanation: Ezekiel does get an assignment like that elsewhere, so I see where it came from. But in this verse, God says, "Clap your hands, stomp your feet, and cry out ‘Alas!’…" (Ezekiel 6:11) It's hands and feet and a shout, not lying down. This is a message he acts out loudly.

Not this time, friend. God says, "He who is far off will die by the plague, he who is near will fall by the sword, and he who remains will die by famine." (Ezekiel 6:12) Far off doesn't mean safe here. The far one falls to plague, the near one to the sword, and the one who remains to famine.

Right, baker. God says, "He who is far off will die by the plague, he who is near will fall by the sword, and he who remains will die by famine." (Ezekiel 6:12) Far off, near, or left behind, each one is named. Distance doesn't get anybody out of this picture.

explanations.answer: Offered fragrant incense to their idols
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The verse ends by calling them "the places where they offered fragrant incense to all their idols." (Ezekiel 6:13) So the hills, mountaintops and leafy oaks were the very spots of their idol worship. That's where the slain will lie.

explanations.answer: Hid from the armies of their enemies
explanations.explanation: Hiding in the hills sounds sensible, but that isn't what the verse says. It calls them "the places where they offered fragrant incense to all their idols." (Ezekiel 6:13) So these were worship spots, not hideouts. The slain will lie among the idols there.

explanations.answer: Built homes for their growing families
explanations.explanation: Homes would be a nice thought, but the verse has something else in mind. It calls them "the places where they offered fragrant incense to all their idols." (Ezekiel 6:13) The high hills and leafy oaks were where they burned incense to idols. That's why the slain lie there.
